name: Carrot maxxing
lead: Carrot maxxing is the looksmaxxing practice of eating large amounts of carrots or other carotenoid-rich foods to give the skin a golden or orange tint. It relies on carotenemia (also called carotenosis), a documented, benign condition in which excess dietary carotenoids accumulate in the outer skin layer [1][2].

Medical literature on carotenemia is largely clinical: case descriptions, reviews and differential diagnosis, with emphasis on distinguishing it from jaundice [1][2]. No clinical studies have tested it as a cosmetic technique.
infobox: Fades over weeks to months after intake stops

paras: Wikipedia describes carotenosis as a harmless, reversible orange discolouration of the skin due to excess carotenoids, most visible in light-skinned people and often most noticeable on palms, soles, knees and nasolabial folds; it spares the whites of the eyes, which helps distinguish it from jaundice [1]. Intake above roughly 20 mg per day of beta-carotene is described as likely to cause it, with colour taking about four to seven weeks to appear [1]. A related condition from lycopene is also described [1][4].

Medical reviews note that carrots and other yellow vegetables are the usual cause and that the condition matters mainly because it can be confused with jaundice [2]. Carotenemia also occurs in association with some diseases and conditions, including hypothyroidism, diabetes and anorexia nervosa [1][5].

A 1983 JAMA report described ten women with anovulation, nine with amenorrhea, who had diet-induced carotenemia and ate pure or predominantly vegetarian diets [6]. The report does not establish that carotenemia itself is the cause. Wikipedia states carotenosis itself is generally considered harmless and typically fades over several months after high intake stops [1].
No studies found on carrot maxxing as a cosmetic practice. Clinical literature on carotenemia exists, consisting of case reports and reviews focused on diagnosis [2][7].

timeline.event: Observations on carotenemia published in Annals of Internal Medicine [7].
Lycopenemia described as a variant of carotenemia in the New England Journal of Medicine [4].
A review of carotenemia published in Clinical Pediatrics [2].

card.summary: Eating lots of carrots to tint the skin orange-gold; carotenemia is real but takes weeks and is a medical curiosity.
card.note: Orange skin can be mistaken for jaundice; it has been associated with some medical conditions.

quick.overview:
Carrot maxxing means eating lots of carrots or similar foods to give the skin a golden or orange tone. The effect it relies on, carotenemia, is real and documented.

However, the literature treats it as a harmless oddity to be told apart from jaundice, not as a cosmetic method, and no trials exist.
quick.mechanism: Carotenoids from food accumulate in the outer skin layer. Wikipedia says colour typically appears after several weeks of high intake and fades over months after stopping.
quick.risks: Carotenemia is generally described as benign, but it can mimic jaundice and is also associated with certain conditions such as hypothyroidism and eating disorders. A report described amenorrhea in women with diet-induced carotenemia.
